sections.title: 2.1 COLREGS Concepts
sections.text:
The COLREGS contain 41 rules to ensure safe maritime trafic in open seas. While ports involve often busy maritime trafic, only a limited number of vessels (typically 2-6) are involved in open sea encounters [43, 76, 85]. Moreover, in busy waters close to shorelines, local trafic separation schemes, which override COLREGS, are often used. Rules 1–19, covering steering and sailing, and Rules 21–22, focusing on light placement, shapes, and visibility requirements, are the most relevant for evaluating the safety of ASV control systems. The remaining rules primarily cover administrative and operational details concerning lighting and shapes for specific vessel types and specialized situations. This section discusses the rules relevant for the scope of this study. • Rule 6: Safe speed: Vessels must maintain a "safe speed" at all times, but COLREGS ofer limited guidance on this. While moderating speed is critical in restricted visibility (e.g., fog) [14], in good visibility and open sea conditions, "safe speed" is typically the vessel’s cruising speed. Table 1. TS1 is overtaking OS, OS and TS2 are head-on, OS is crossing TS3 from port. • Rule 7: Risk of collision: A course is defined by the vessel’s constant speed and heading. According to the COLREGS, a risk of collision exists when two vessels are on a collision course, i.e., without any intervention, they will likely collide in the future. • Rule 8: Action to avoid collision: This rule emphasizes maintaining a "safe distance" and making "readily apparent" course changes. A safe distance generally means a significant enough distance between the vessels so that hydrodynamic efects cannot lead to contact. It is often approximated by a convex area around the vessel called the safety domain. Some commonly used elliptical safety domains are mentioned in [15, 18, 60, 69, 77]. For course changes to be "readily apparent", common practice based on case law and custom [78] suggests a change of at least 30◦. • Rule 11: Deemed COLREGS situations: Rule 11 indicates that the specific positions and velocities determine each ship’s collision avoidance responsibilities when the vessels first get within the visibility range [35]. These responsibilities are detailed by Rules 12-18 (see Section 2.2). • Rule 22: Visibility range: The visibility range of a vessel is usually between 1 and 6 nautical miles (NM) based on the required range and beam angle of positional lights, depending on ship size.

Analogously to previous work on scenario generation for autonomous driving [3, 51], COL-REGS compliance can investigated on multiple abstraction levels in a maritime context [41]. System-level ASV testing is carried out using simulators that execute concrete scenarios as test cases consisting of initial scenes, and detailed trajectories for all target ships. The initial scene marks the start of a scenario, typically when two vessels first come into visibility range. Then, the trajectory of each vessel determines its position, heading, and speed at a specific point in time. An initial scene for an open sea encounter of vessels must satisfy various geometrical and numerical constraints (e.g., relative bearing in a crossing encounter), represented by logical scenarios. Each initial scene represents one solution of the set of constraints defined by a logical scenario. In this paper, a logical scenario represents a potentially dangerous multi-vessel COLREGS-regulated encounter, which sets the ASV and one or more target ships on a potential collision course. For a s stematic investi ation of semanticall diferent COLREGS situations that involve a certain number of target ships, functional scenarios can be derived from logical scenarios by qualitative abstraction (QA) [4]. Using qualitative abstraction, one can derive a graph model (based on relational algebra) to represent functional scenarios by abstracting geometrical constraints between vessels into high-level relations such as "crossing from port situation". abstract: Autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) need to complete missions without posing risks to other maritime traffic. Safe traffic in open sea encounters is controlled by the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) formulated by the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Designed with human operators in mind, the COLREGS are intentionally underspecified, which may result in ambiguous requirements for correct behaviour for ASVs. Hence the systematic testing of such ambiguous situations is particularly important. This paper investigates to what extent existing test scenario generation approaches deemed effective in the automotive domain can be adapted to test COLREGS-compliance in a maritime context with multi-vessel encounters. In a series of experiments involving synthetic and real-world test scenarios, their performance is evaluated with respect to relevance, diversity, completeness, scalability and speed. Our results indicate that (1) test scenarios derived from historic maritime traffic are insufficient for testing multi-ship encounters. Moreover, (2) existing test scenario generation techniques provide sufficient scalability and speed, but they are very limited in terms of diversity and completeness when the number of vessels increases.

Metrics. Unfortunately, no generally accepted metrics exist which would measure the relevance of a test suite for assessing COLREGS-compliance. However, a minimum requirement for relevance is that the ships in a test scenario are actually in a COLREGS-scenario (see Section 2.2). Furthermore, ambiguous scenarios are known to be relevant for system-level testing in the maritime domain [41]. Hence, for each compared approach, we calculate the ratio of relevant and consistent scenarios $( \mathcal T \cap C )$ with respect to the total number of generated scenes.
